rationale: A wins because it keeps the heat where the facts are: "Peloton is calling itself profitable. Its own numbers disagree." is the cleanest editor-safe tension in the update. B has the same broad menu, but "The company everyone wrote off..." and "Peloton is dead" lean on an invented consensus; that is not contrarian, it is unsourced theater. A still needs a few sharper caveats, but it gives a founder usable routes without making a reporter clean up unsupported premises.
gaps_in_A: "How Peloton's new CEO manufactured its first profitable quarter in three years" uses "manufactured" like there is accounting smoke. The facts support cost cuts and adjusted EBITDA/free cash flow, not manipulation.

"first profitable quarter" needs the adjusted/net-income caveat closer to the headline in the exec angle. A finance reporter will not let that slide just because the contrarian angle handles it later.

"business reporter covering corporate turnarounds and executive leadership" is directionally right but still a little broad. It needs a tighter outlet lane, such as public-company turnaround, retail restructuring, or consumer discretionary earnings.
"Next step: find-journalists" jumps one beat early. First pick the angle whose proof actually exists this week; then build the list.
gaps_in_B: "The company everyone wrote off" invents market consensus. The update gives Peloton's quarter, not proof that everyone had written it off.
"The prevailing belief is that pandemic-era connected-fitness winners are in permanent decline" is outside context presented as fact. If you cannot cite coverage or analyst sentiment, cut it.
"Record-low churn is doing more for Peloton than any new bike" asserts a comparison the update never supports, and "any new bike" is not in the facts.
"a clean cause-and-effect candidate" overplays the churn story. The set later says not to imply causation, but the angle has already put the banana peel on the floor.
